text: Diane Crump (May 18, 1948 – January 1, 2026) was an American jockey and horse trainer. On February 7, 1969, she became the first woman to compete as a professional jockey in a pari-mutuel race in the United States, riding a horse named Bridle 'n Bit at Hialeah Park Race Track. Her participation faced intense hostility, requiring a full police escort through an angry crowd of shouting people, with hecklers yelling things like "Go back to the kitchen and cook dinner." Crump finished 9th in the 12-horse race and later recalled that her excitement allowed her to overcome the negative attitudes of male jockeys, trainers, and owners. Two weeks later, she won her first race. She was inspired to apply for a jockey's license in the fall of 1968 after Kathryn Kusner, the first woman licensed as a jockey, won a lawsuit against the Maryland Racing Commission for gender-based denial of a license; although Kusner was injured shortly after receiving her license, Crump stepped forward. Throughout 1968, female jockeys faced significant resistance; for example, W. L. Lyons Brown, a part owner of Churchill Downs, requested Crump not compete there due to anticipated controversy, and Penny Ann Early was denied the chance to ride because male jockeys boycotted her races. Two other women had been forced out of races after male jockeys threw rocks at their trailers and threatened a boycott. The situation at Hialeah changed when track officials threatened sanctions against male jockeys. In 1970, Crump became the first woman to ride in the Kentucky Derby, winning the first race on the undercard and finishing 15th in a 17-horse field on a horse named Fathom. By the time she retired from racing in 1985, she had ridden to 235 wins, though Equibase officially credits her with 228. She received invitations to ride in Puerto Rico and Venezuela; in a 1970s Puerto Rican race, she hit a male jockey with her whip after he held onto her saddle, and he eventually pulled away to win. On February 1, 1989, Crump suffered a serious riding accident in which she was crushed under her horse, breaking her leg in six or seven places, her ankle, and ribs, requiring ten days in the hospital and leading doctors to say she would never ride again. After recovery, she returned to riding, but accumulated injuries over the years ultimately led to her permanent retirement in 1999. She briefly retired in 1985 to focus on family, working as a farm trainer at Calumet Farm in Lexington, Kentucky, for over three years, and later trained horses at the Middleburg Training Center in Virginia starting in 1991. She resumed riding in 1992 and competed through 1998 before retiring in 1999. She ran an equine sales business and lived in Virginia. Crump was married to trainer Don Divine from 1969 to 1987. In 2020, a biography titled Diane Crump: A Horse Racing Pioneer's Life in the Saddle by Mark Shrager was published. In 2025, she was diagnosed with glioblastoma, and her family launched a GoFundMe to cover medical expenses. She died on January 1, 2026, in Winchester, Virginia, at the age of 77.
